nodes.author: haridigresses
nodes.text:
This is a fascinating case study for both founders and those seeking to understand founder mentality.

Jack & Airwallex could have sold for $1.2B to Stripe in 2018. At the time, Stripe was worth $20B. Let's say Jack gets $400-500M from that sale (rest goes to cofounders, investors, employees); Stripe has >4xed since then (hence his comment that he would have netted out >$2B today).

Airwallex is worth $8B today. With dilution, Jack probably owns $2-2.5B max.

Commentators observe: "doesn't sound like a great deal... you busted your ass for another 7 years didn't end up ahead."

This completely misses the point. The entirety of the motivation for some of the best founders is to "put a dent in the universe".

If Airwallex had exited at $1.2B, then Jack would have the pride of putting a very-solid dent in the universe. 99th percentile outcome.

But
- What if you have greater ambitions? What if you want a 99.99th percentile dent?
- If the international business thrives from there... who is responsible for the "rest of the dent"? Airwallex or Stripe? Everything 2018 onwards is to the Collisons' credit, not Jack. There's probably a good bit of pride in wanting *your* dent to be bigger.
- Great, you sell. What then? What is your next purpose? Start a new company? Starting from 0 is REALLY not fun... why wouldn't you just take the so-rare PMF you've already achieved, and scale it from there?
- Finally and most importantly, it's NOT about the money. After a certain figure (which is $100M for some, $1B for some, $10M for some or even less), it's diminishing returns. After that it's about impact, meaning, and the thrill of the hunt: the next ridiculous milestone, the next ambitious goal, the next impossible dent.

Hindsight is 20/20. A lot of founders would say "I wish I'd taken it."

But just as many would say "It didn't work out, and I had the opportunity to cash out along the way... but I don't regret a thing. I'm glad I took the biggest possible swing."

This is why VC is a great match for the most ridiculously ambitious founders. As @bgurley said "Venture capital is not even a home-run business. It's a grand-slam business." Many great founders feel the same way.

nodes.author: T_h_eWordsmith
nodes.text:
This company almost died 3 times before hitting $1B ARR and raising $330M in revenue.

Jack (@awxjack) could’ve announced that milestone like every other founder does:

 “We just crossed $1B ARR. Its a huge milestone for us…”

But NO, he didn’t.

He chose to tell the story of how they got there. The part most founders hide:

➠ how he lost all financial support at 16

➠ how he worked 12-hour shifts under 40°C heat while still coding and building a solution for a problem he saw (global payments)

➠ how they got their first $1M investment  from someone who believed in him before the company even existed.

➠ the company almost failing 3 different times

➠ how they turned down Stripe’s $1.2B offer because the team still believed in their vision

And how they eventually reached the milestone after years of burn out and setbacks 

When you read that, you don’t see pity.

You see resilience
You see humanity
You see a founder who didn’t give up even when everything was against him.

And the impact was crazy:

Founders, investors, media brands, users, and huge accounts shared the post with people dropping their positive sentiments commending their journey. 

The story blew up and all that visibility, trust and attention went straight back to @airwallex  through Jack’s voice.

Because that’s the thing a lot of founders forget:

In DeFi, fintech, payments,  anything involving money, trust is everything.

And people trust people before products.

Jack even admitted that for 10 years, he didn’t talk about what he was building.

He thought staying invisible was best at the time.

But being invisible has a price:

Customers don’t know you exist

And founders with smaller or worse products get 10x more attention

If there's anything to take from this, it's simple:

Your journey as a founder or co-founder isn't a weakness.

It's part of your brand.

And people connect better with the human behind the product.

nodes.author: aakashgupta
nodes.text:
The real story here isn’t the Stripe rejection.

It’s that Zhang built a $1.2 million coffee shop problem into an $8 billion company by being constitutionally incapable of playing it safe.

Lucy Liu met Zhang once at his Melbourne cafe in 2015. By the end of dinner she offered $2 million for 40% of a company that didn’t exist yet. Zhang negotiated her down to $1 million for 20%. The next Monday, the money hit his personal bank account. He hadn’t even quit his day job.

That $1 million is now worth roughly $800 million. A 800x return from a single dinner.

But here’s what nobody talks about: Zhang’s first two products completely failed. The peer-to-peer FX model couldn’t generate enough volume. The invoicing product spooked customers who thought payment requests were phishing scams. By late 2016 he had six weeks of runway and no plan B.

His solution? Cold call Macquarie Bank until someone picked up. A random sales guy on the FX desk said yes.

This pattern repeated. Sequoia China said they’d only invest if Tencent joined. Tencent’s investment committee approved, then Pony Ma personally killed the deal. Zhang spent two months chasing James Mitchell during Christmas vacation. Got the meeting January 5th. Demo crashed. Mitchell invested anyway.

Zhang once showed up to the office unable to feel half his body. Too much stress. His cofounders slapped his face and he felt nothing. Doctors confirmed it was psychosomatic.

The $8 billion valuation yesterday? That’s the outcome of someone who treats “six weeks from bankruptcy” as a normal operating condition.

$1 billion ARR. $235 billion transaction volume. 80 licenses in 200+ countries. Clients include Brex, Rippling, Canva, SHEIN.

Zhang says he still hasn’t done anything that makes him proud. His goal is to surpass Citi and HSBC within 15 years.

Conviction is a hell of a drug.

🤯 This company literally turned down Stripe’s $1.2B offer in 2018, now they’re at $1B ARR. This is the story of Jack Zhang and his company Airwallex...

Airwallex, a Singapore-headquartered fintech company founded in 2015 in Melbourne, Australia, builds financial infrastructure for global businesses, starting with cross-border payments and expanding into accounts, cards, treasury, and expense tools. By late 2025, it serves over 150,000 customers like TikTok and Canva, with $800 million in annual recurring revenue and $130 billion in processed payments. 

Founding CEO Jack Zhang, who immigrated from China to Australia as a teen and supported himself through factory and service jobs, co-founded Airwallex with Jacob Dai (CTO), Max Li (Head of Design), Lucy Liu (President), and Ki-lok Wong. The idea emerged while Zhang and Li ran a coffee shop, Tukk & Co., and faced high fees importing supplies from China via traditional banks like Western Union. Bootstrapped with personal investments including $1 million from Liu, the team coded relentlessly in a tiny office before launching in beta.

Airwallex joined Mastercard's accelerator in 2016, raised $13 million in Series A from Tencent and Sequoia by 2017, and rejected a $1.2 billion Stripe acquisition offer in 2018 despite low revenue. It hit $1 billion in payment volume that year and scaled rapidly via API products for faster, cheaper international transfers.

Recent expansions include startup grants, entry into France, and IPO preparations for 2026, with a $6.2 billion valuation after $1.2 billion in funding.

九死一生的创业：3次濒临倒闭-->80亿美元

真正的故事不在于被Stripe拒绝。

而在于张这个人——他骨子里就没有“求稳”这个选项，硬是把一个120万美元的咖啡馆难题，做成了一家80亿美元的公司。

2015年，Lucy在墨尔本他的咖啡馆见了张一面。一顿饭还没吃完，她就提出：用一个当时还不存在的公司40%的股份，换她200万美元投资。张把条件谈成了：100万美元，换20%的股份。紧接着的周一，钱就打进了他的个人账户。那时，他甚至还没辞掉他的全职工作。

那100万美元，现在价值大约8亿美元。一顿饭，800倍的回报。

但没人谈论的是：张的前两个产品彻底失败了。P2P外汇模式做不起量；发票产品把客户吓跑了，他们以为付款请求是钓鱼诈骗。到2016年底，公司资金只剩六周，没有B计划。

他的解决办法？不停地给麦格理银行打冷电话，直到有人接听。 外汇部门一个随机的销售小哥说了“行”。

这个模式不断重复。红杉中国说，除非腾讯跟投，否则他们不投。腾讯投委会批了，但马化腾亲自否决了交易。张花了两个月，在圣诞假期追着詹姆斯·米切尔。终于在1月5号见了面。产品演示当场崩溃。米切尔还是投了。

张曾有一次到办公室时，半边身体失去了知觉。压力太大了。他的联合创始人扇他耳光，他什么感觉都没有。医生确认这是身心性症状。

昨天80亿美元的估值？这就是一个把 “离破产还有六周” 视为常态运营条件的人，所得到的结果。

10亿美元年度经常性收入。2.35万亿美元交易额。在200多个国家持有80个牌照。客户包括Brex、Rippling、Canva、SHEIN。

张说，他至今还没做出任何让自己感到自豪的事。他的目标是在15年内超越花旗和汇丰。

信念这东西，真是让人上瘾。

nodes.author: T_h_eWordsmith
nodes.text:
Last year, I did a short breakdown of @airwallex  journey to hitting $1B ARR.

and how the founder chose to tell the story rather than giving a regular announcement, causing the founders' post to reach;

46M+ people with many positive, trust building engagement from their target audience.

Now, I'm going to show you exactly why the post worked and how you can replicate it as a founder or ghostwriter 🧵

──── ◁ II ▷ ────

The first step is to: 

1 ➠ Start with your origin: 

This could be a major challenge you faced while building, a problem you noticed, your background before building, or an experience that changed everything. 

>> This is the human side that pulls people in to hear you. 

@airwallex founder didn't share the win straight. 

before the $1B ARR, before the $330M raise, he took us back to: 

losing financial support early, working brutal jobs, and struggling to survive while building

That immediately changed how the win was perceived.

2. ➠ Show the problem before the product: 

Airwallex founder shared the payment problem he discovered as friction he personally felt while running a coffee business.

This made the product look like the best response to that problem. 

After your origin story, don’t rush into what you built, but rather zoom in on the problem you noticed  or experienced that refused to go away.

When you go from your struggles >>  problems, the solution (your product) begins to make sense why it exists. 

 3. ➠ Show belief in what you're building:

This could come in many ways, but when people see how much you are willing to push for your product, trust flows in naturally.

Airwallex founder showed his by sharing how he turned down stripes $1.2B offer, which was a decision under pressure but due to his co-founders belief in what they were building. 

That single belief did more for trust than any metric ever could. 

4. ➠ Share the win:
This is where you finally share the win in your story. 

Airwallex founder shared how their journey led to them hitting $1B ARR before the $330M raise. 

Your win doesn't have to be a massive revenue record (depends on what you want to share)

It could be: 

⤷ The transformation your product is now bringing to users.

⤷ The increased adoption of your product in xyz regions or among xyz target audience. 

⤷ User growth, etc.

5. ➠ Tie the past to the future:

Don't end the content with your win. 

Airwallex founder ended at “here’s what we’re building toward next.”

Thats what turns your origin story into positioning. 

By sharing what the future looks like for you, your product, or brand, you give your audience (who now trust you) a future to look forward to. 

If you strip it down, the framework looks like this:

→Origin → Your journey 
→Problem → Problem you noticed 
→ Belief anchor → The process
→ Outcome/win → The proof 
→ Future Direction → What comes next 

This content framework turns your founder journey into a belief and trust engine.

nodes.author: Wuhuoqiu
nodes.text:
之前我跟@YettaSing都分享过一个观点，那就是当前市场虽然不好，但创业方向确实最清晰的一届，稳定币支付，预测市场，万物上链这些都是新蓝海，且确定有PMF的路径，强力的团队在这几个赛道上做出不错的产品，肯定能拿到融资，也肯定会有人用，最终成不成功是Another Story，但至少不会沦为上一轮的纯叙事盘。

想起来二三年我跟一个老外BTC L2团队聊，他们是做“BTC EVM Rollup的”，我当时问Founder，你都Rollup了，为啥非要Roll去BTC呢，ETH不行么？而且ETH上面好多个EVM Rollup的L2了，你Roll去BTC的理由是啥，BTC L1也不支持智能合约。他回答，BTC比ETH更安全! 我 - “……”

现在这种项目应该是很难再骗到融资了，无论是VC还是散户都不买单，未来市场买单的应该就是我说的那种，能跟现实世界产生互动，对传统金融降本增效的项目

这不今儿看到 @yzilabs 领投的 @allscaleio 数字银行，就是走的这种路线。看完他们视频介绍，感觉至少走在了正确的道路上。去年底我预测的这一轮三个主线方向 - PayFI，AI Agent，Meme，应该或多或少跟团队是想到了一起

首先如果你认同小毛哥@porounclemao的超级个体理论的话（什么，你没看过，赶紧去小毛哥X上学习一下），哪怕你没看过，在AI越来越强的现如今，你应该不会怀疑，过去那种动辄几千上万人的公司，未来会越来越少。而现在几十个人或者十几人的小公司，将来可能真的就是三五个人甚至一个人就能把活搞定。未来10-20年，一定会出现越来越多的freelancer，其中不乏能力超强的那种超级个体。这些人借助AI，可以在任何地方任何时间，把你委托的活干好，而他们可能来自中国，美国，也可能是来自非洲，南美这些欠发达地区，毕竟只要有手机有网络，AI就可以服务每个人

那么问题来了，当全球性freelancer撑起越来越多经济活动和GDP的时候，其中支付以及支付相关的各种事宜该咋弄？Stripe/Airwallex吧 - 开户门槛高、审核严格、随时可能封号，传统银行就不说了，到账周期长（3-7天），手续费高（2.9%+），且全球仍有14亿成年人没有银行账户。Crypto当然是最佳选择，但你总不能指望所有的经济活动都跟KOL接广子一样，“老师给个EVM地址”，然后发过去，打钱。不是每个Freelancer都有币安账户，也不是每个人都会用Metamask和Phantom，更不用提成熟的经济活动你至少得牵扯Invoice，交易历史，法币出入金等一系列配套设施

拿旅游这个最常见的场景来说，23年那会ABCDE巴厘岛团建，我去之前事先下载了Wise，以应付当地的一些刷卡需求。但在给出租车司机，酒店服务人员和外卖小哥的小费时候，还是不得已在机场换了一些美元和当地的印尼盾来用，经常用完了小额的遇见一个意外需要小费的时刻尴尬，有时候不得已就直接给个大额的。当时我就在想你能给我个币安UID或者钱包二维码不？我给你转2U小费！

但可能么？至少那会，甚至包括现在都不太现实

一言以蔽之，让全球任何人都能在几分钟内用稳定币收付款，无需银行账户，无需复杂的助记词，迅速开具一个Invoice，这个生态位依旧是缺失的

Allscale本质就是做的这个事情，不要把他理解成一个钱包，理解成一个轻量的链上数字银行更为贴切

1. 支持USDT/USDC即时收款，秒级到账
2. 无账户封禁风险，真正的自托管（passkey生成链上地址，系统不保存私钥）
3. 一键生成带税率、折扣、备注的专业Invoice，客户无需持有crypto也能付款
4. 专为"轻量经营活动"设计的跨境收付款工作台
目前已与Skill Afrika（非洲最大自由职业者社区）等多个非洲社区达成深度合作，下个月即将进入南美市场，Gas费用封顶或补贴，让每一笔几美元的交易不会因网络波动变得不可控

除了Yzi Labs领投，团队实力也很强，技术上有负责IBM、Amazon等大公司全球收款与账户体系架构人才，合规上有Square TBD项目负责crypto支付合规和Kraken的Krak稳定币数字银行经验，产品上有来自TikTok、Capital One的资深产品经理，算得上六边形团队。市场扩张层面，AllScale 展现出了极强的战术素养。团队汇聚了全球市场营销的资深操盘手，他们深谙 HP 的渠道销售（Channel Sales）扩张之道，懂得如何通过合作伙伴快速通过 B 端渗透市场；同时兼具 Dell 的直销模式（Direct Sales）基因，能以极高的效率直接触达全球SMB用户。

正如有了银行和Visa，电商时代我们依旧诞生了Paypal。现有的Crypto Infra已经趋向成熟，但在支付领域依旧缺乏一个类似Paypal这样可以真正触达海量Freelancer和商家的“消费级支付应用 + 商户支付解决方案”，Allscale至少走在了这样一条正确的道路上。现在刚刚上线了ASP积分系统，大家通过完成注册邀请签到支付这些简单的动作就可以拿到积分，撸毛的同时顺便自己真的可以用起来，何乐而不为呢

nodes.author: rabois
nodes.text:
To recap: in 2015, two parallel payment networks were launched – both designed to bypass SWIFT.

• October 2015: the People’s Bank of China activates the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to “provide clearing and settlement for cross-border RMB” and reduce reliance on SWIFT.
• December 2015: four founders raised in China incorporate @Airwallex in Melbourne, describing it as a “proprietary global network in parallel to SWIFT.”

Ten years later…
> Airwallex routes payments for tens of thousands of U.S. companies, including AI labs, defense contractors, and financial institutions.
> Roughly 40% of its 2,000 employees work in mainland China and Hong Kong, many in engineering roles that “design and maintain mission-critical payment systems.”
> Those employees and executives fall under the PRC National Intelligence Law (Arts. 7 & 10) and Hong Kong National Security Law, both of which require cooperation with state-security requests and prohibit disclosure.
> The company’s Chinese investors – Tencent, HongShan (formerly Sequoia China), and others – hold more than 20% of equity.
> Airwallex (Guangzhou) is one of only two “foreign” companies to hold a PBOC-issued payment license, integrating it into domestic Chinese clearing systems.

On December 8, 2025, the Australian Financial Review reported that an Airwallex executive warned internally that requests for wider customer-data access were originating from staff in China. And the company separately announced a “dual global headquarters” in San Francisco to fuel continued U.S. expansion. No major corporate officers seem to live in SF.

Beijing’s 2024–25 policy line calls for building a “自主可控的跨境支付体系” – an autonomous, controllable cross-border payment system.
Again this morning, Airwallex’s CEO told CNBC: “We built a global network in parallel to the SWIFT system… applying AI agents to create full autonomous finance.”

Same year, same goal, same vocabulary.
A company founded by Chinese nationals, majority-engineered in China, primarily owned by Chinese investors, and operating under Chinese law has become a de facto non-SWIFT payments network and now moves financial data for thousands of U.S. and global firms in critical industries.

Airwallex doesn’t just compete with SWIFT – it completes Beijing’s plan to see inside it.

The result: a Western-facing fintech that doubles as a lawful intelligence window into sensitive U.S. companies.

nodes.author: sytaylor
nodes.text:
Airwallex just raised $330M at an $8B valuation.

The numbers first:
- $1B+ annualized revenue (up 90% YoY)
- $235B+ in transaction volume
- HQ moving from Melbourne to San Francisco

This is the biggest B2B payments company most Americans haven't heard of.

These are incredible numbers.

But there's some social media drama drowning out this success.

And ironically now most Americans *have* heard of Airwallex...

---

Keith Rabois called them a "Chinese backdoor" into US corporate data.

Jack Ma say's we're complying with data residency laws.

But that's not the full story.

—

Rabois raised a legitimate question.

China's National Intelligence Law *can* compel companies to assist state intelligence.

Airwallex *does* have engineers in Shanghai.

Tencent *is* an investor.

For companies handling sensitive financial data, jurisdictional risk is worth scrutinizing.

—

Airwallex's response was equally direct:
- US data stored only in US/Singapore
- Chinese engineers don't have production data access
- SOC2 compliant, independently audited

These are verifiable claims. Not PR spin.

So why attack Airwallex?

My guess? Defending turf of existing portco's 

—

What I think gets lost in the Twitter drama:

Airwallex and Stripe (or Brex, or Ramp) aren't really the same product.

Stripe is developer-first payments for internet businesses.

Airwallex is multi-rail treasury infrastructure for companies operating across borders—the CFO tool for managing 20+ local clearing systems, FX, and cross-border settlement.

Different buyer. 

Different starting place. 

Sort of different market.

Some overlapping products. Especially as Airwallex comes to the US. 

—

The harder industry question:

If we apply strict "no offshore engineering" rules to fintech, we'd lose a significant chunk of the global supply chain. Many US fintechs have distributed teams.

But if we ignore jurisdictional nuance entirely, we're naive.

The real answer is probably boring: auditable code review processes, data residency attestations, third-party verification.

Compliance work that doesn't fit in a tweet.

—

Airwallex is now worth $8B because CFOs at mid-market multinationals care about settlement times and FX spreads.

The geopolitical debate is worth having.

But don't let that distract you from the business underneath that is executing.

Rabois may have given Airwallex great free marketing by taking a shot.

The top-view list shifted toward the Stripe-rejection hook and debate over the implied valuation/revenue trade-off. @Austen’s quote reached about 1.96M views, while @aakashgupta’s reached about 125K; several critique posts also accumulated substantial views.

The search results also included a pre-anchor Airwallex milestone post by @sytaylor at approximately -90 minutes, so the launch conversation had some precursor activity before the anchor.

Second-wave quote expansion was attempted for 1998036050770636932 and 1998060890978242648. The returned quote trees were mostly much later, low-engagement generic reactions or unrelated creator content; no substantial additional second-wave narrative cluster was recovered.
